units.title: Component 01: Living in the UK Today

outcomes.text: Describe where upland, lowland and glaciated landscapes are found in the UK.
Describe the geology, climate and human activity that characterise these landscapes.
Define the types of weathering, mass movement, erosion, transport and deposition.
Explain how waterfalls, gorges, V-shaped valleys, floodplains, levees, meanders and ox-bow lakes form along a river basin.
Explain how headlands, bays, caves, arches, stacks, beaches and spits form.

subtopics.title: UK river and coast case studies

outcomes.text: Use a UK river basin and a UK coastal case study to show how geomorphic processes work at different scales and are shaped by geology and climate.
Describe the landforms and features found in each case study.
Explain how human activity, including management, works with geomorphic processes to affect the landscape.
Outline the UK's major trading partners, with its main exports and imports.
Describe geographical patterns of employment, income, life expectancy, education, ethnicity and broadband access in the UK.
Explain the causes of uneven development in the UK: location, economic change, infrastructure and government policy.
Use a case study of one UK place or region to describe the consequences of economic growth or decline.
Describe changes in the UK's population structure since 1900 and its position on the Demographic Transition Model.
Explain the causes, effects and responses to an ageing population.
Outline immigration flows into the UK this century and their social and economic impacts.
Explain the causes of suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation and re-urbanisation.
Outline the social, economic and environmental consequences of these urban trends.
Use a UK city case study to explain the city's place in its region, the country and the world.
Explain how migration shapes the city's growth and character.
Describe ways of life in the city: culture, ethnicity, housing, leisure and consumption.
Describe challenges of housing, transport and waste, and a sustainable strategy for one of them.
Explain how air masses, the North Atlantic Drift and continentality influence UK weather.
Explain how air masses cause extremes of wind, temperature and precipitation.
For one UK flood caused by extreme weather, describe its causes, including the weather conditions.
Describe the flood's effects on people and the environment and how it was managed at different scales.
Describe how humans modify UK environments for food (mechanised farming, commercial fishing), energy (wind farms, fracking) and water (reservoirs, transfer schemes).
Identify renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
Describe how much each contributes to UK energy supply.
Describe changing UK energy supply and demand since 1950 and the role of government and international organisations.
Evaluate strategies for sustainable energy use and management at local and national scales.
Describe renewable energy development in the UK and its impacts on people and the environment.
Discuss the extent to which non-renewable energy should supply the UK's future.
Explain the economic, political and environmental factors affecting future UK energy supply.
Describe abiotic and biotic ecosystem components and how they are interdependent.
Describe the global distribution of polar regions, coral reefs, grasslands, temperate forests, tropical rainforests and hot deserts.
Describe the climate, plants and animals of these ecosystems.
Locate the major tropical rainforests: Amazon, Central American, Congo Basin, Madagascan, South East Asian and Australasian.
Locate the major warm water coral reefs, including the Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea, New Caledonia, Mesoamerican, Florida and Andros reefs.
Explain nutrient and water cycles within tropical rainforests.
Explain nutrient cycling within coral reefs.
Use a rainforest and a coral reef case study to show interdependence of climate, soil, water, plants, animals and humans.
Explain the value of these ecosystems to humans and the planet.
Describe threats to biodiversity and efforts to reduce them through sustainable use and management.
Give social, economic and environmental definitions of development, including sustainable development.
Describe development indicators (GNI per capita, Human Development Index, Internet users) with their strengths and weaknesses.
Explain how indicators show the consequences of uneven development.
Describe the current pattern of advanced countries, emerging and developing countries and low-income developing countries.
Outline reasons for uneven development, including colonialism's effect on trade and exploitation of resources.
Describe types of aid and how aid can both promote and hinder development.

subtopics.title: An LIDC or EDC case study

outcomes.text: Use a case study of one LIDC or EDC to show how its location, environment, politics, trade, investment, population, employment, social factors, technology and an aid project shape its development.
Use Rostow's model to judge the country's path of economic development.
Define city, megacity and world city.
Describe the distribution of megacities and how it has changed.
Explain how urban growth rates vary between areas of different development.
Explain the causes of rapid urbanisation in LIDCs: push and pull factors and natural growth.
Outline its social, economic and environmental consequences.

subtopics.title: A major LIDC or EDC city

outcomes.text: Use a case study of one major LIDC or EDC city to explain its place in its region, the country and the world.
Explain how migration shapes the city's growth and character.
Describe ways of life in the city: culture, ethnicity, housing, leisure and consumption.
Describe challenges of housing, transport and waste, and a sustainable strategy for one of them.
Describe how climate has changed since the Quaternary began, including ice ages.
Describe warming and cooling periods since 1000AD: medieval warming, Little Ice Age and modern warming.
Describe evidence for climate change: temperature data, ice cores, tree rings, paintings and diaries.
Explain natural causes of climate change: solar variation, orbital changes and volcanic activity.
Explain how human activity causes the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.
Summarise consequences of climate change being experienced around the planet.
Describe the distribution of the world's main climatic regions.
Outline how air movement between poles and equator drives the global circulation.
Explain how global circulation produces extreme wind, temperature and precipitation in different places.
Outline the causes of tropical storms and drought.
Describe their distribution and frequency and whether these have changed over time.
For one El Nino or La Nina drought, explain how the extreme weather develops and leads to drought.
Describe the drought's effects on people and the environment.
Describe how people have adapted to the drought.
Select, adapt and construct maps with suitable scales and annotations.
Interpret cross-sections and transects.
Use coordinates, scale and distance.
Extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate map information.
Use gradient, contour and spot height on OS and other isoline maps.
Describe, interpret and analyse geo-spatial data in a GIS.
Use atlas, OS (1:50 000 and 1:25 000), base, choropleth, isoline, flow line, desire-line, sphere of influence, thematic, route and sketch maps.
Select, adapt and construct graphs and charts with suitable scales and annotations.
Present and communicate data effectively through graphs and charts.
Extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate information from graphs and charts.

Use bar graphs, histograms, line graphs, scatter graphs with best fit, dispersion graphs, pie charts, climate graphs, proportional symbols, pictograms, cross-sections, population pyramids, radial graphs and rose charts.
Understand number, area and scale, and the quantitative relationships between units.
Use proportion, ratio, magnitude and frequency correctly.
Calculate percentage increase and decrease, and percentiles.
Use median, mean, range, quartiles, inter-quartile range, mode and modal class, and cumulative frequency.
Design fieldwork data collection sheets, considering accuracy, sample size, procedures, control groups and reliability.
Interpret tables of data.
Describe relationships in bivariate data, sketch trend lines and draw estimated lines of best fit.
Make predictions by interpolating and extrapolating trends.
Identify weaknesses in statistical presentations and draw justified conclusions.
Deconstruct, interpret, analyse and evaluate photographs, cartoons, pictures and diagrams.
Analyse written articles for understanding, interpretation and bias.
Suggest improvements, issues or reasons for using maps, graphs, statistics and visual sources.
Understand the kinds of question fieldwork can investigate and the enquiry process used.
Understand fieldwork techniques, including observation and different kinds of measurement.
Process and present fieldwork data in maps, graphs and diagrams.
Analyse and explain field data using geographical case studies and theories.
Draw evidenced conclusions and summaries from fieldwork data.
Reflect critically on fieldwork data, methods, conclusions and knowledge gained.
